summary:
This evaluation covered 11 chat-based EKS compliance tasks run 3 times each (63 iterations total, no failures/errors). One eval ("eks-compliance-smoke-test") was a should_trigger:false test — trigger fired correctly for both variants but expected_output/assertions/comparison were all skipped by design, so it provides no comparative signal.

Across the remaining 10 evals where data exists, a consistent pattern emerges: with_skill met the expected output and passed assertions at or near 100% in nearly every eval, while without_skill's expected-output pass rate was frequently 0/3 or partial (e.g., 0/9, 0/12, 0/15, 0/18, 6/9, 6/12, 8/12, 10/15, 12/15), with two exceptions where both variants fully matched expected output ("eks-compliance-auth-mode-configmap" and "eks-compliance-section3-not-covered," where without_skill still lagged on assertions despite matching overall expected output). Looking at individual assertions rather than aggregates: many assertions passed for both variants equally ("always_passes" pattern — e.g., basic PASS/FAIL calls on well-known controls), showing those checks aren't differentiating the variants. But a recurring "with_skill_passes_without_skill_fails" pattern appears repeatedly across evals, especially on assertions about framework crosswalks (PCI DSS/Security Hub mappings), attestation/certification disclaimers, and specific remediation recommendations (e.g., access entries, kube-bench benchmark naming) — without_skill consistently missed these more nuanced or compliance-framing details. A few assertions were "flaky" for without_skill (e.g., Inspector findings coverage, PCI DSS crosswalk rows), indicating run-to-run variability rather than a hard failure. Confidence in these per-assertion judgments is generally high, though a few expected-output scores for without_skill were rated medium confidence, which tempers certainty in those specific cases.

On cost and runtime, results are mixed and don't uniformly favor one variant: in several evals without_skill was faster/cheaper (e.g., "eks-compliance-denied-read": 2s/$0.02 vs with_skill's 12s/$0.10; "eks-compliance-cis-only-scope": 5s/$0.04 vs 8s/$0.07), but in others without_skill was notably slower and more expensive (e.g., "eks-compliance-live-cis-aws-controls": 1m16s/$0.63 vs with_skill's 37s/$0.31; "eks-compliance-section3-not-covered": 27s/$0.23 vs 11s/$0.09). Context window utilization was similar and low for both (roughly 4-6%) with no compactions.

Quality comparisons (head-to-head LLM judging) were only available for 4 of 11 evals (others skipped the comparison, reducing confidence in quality claims); results were split: with_skill was favored more on completeness, without_skill was favored more on accuracy and actionability in some evals (e.g., "eks-compliance-section3-not-covered," "eks-compliance-live-pci-crosswalk"), while with_skill was favored overall in "eks-compliance-auth-mode-configmap." These quality comparisons carry only medium average confidence.

Output consistency (run-to-run stability) also leans toward with_skill: with_skill was rated "consistent" or "mostly_consistent" in all evals with scores mostly at or near 3.0, while without_skill showed more variability, including one "inconsistent" rating (score 1.0) in "eks-compliance-live-pci-crosswalk" and several "mostly_consistent" ratings with lower scores (2.0-2.33) in evals like "eks-compliance-cis-only-scope" and "eks-compliance-live-cis-aws-controls."

Overall, the dominant signal across this dataset is that with_skill matched expected outputs and assertions more often, particularly on compliance-framework mapping and disclaimer-related criteria, and showed somewhat more run-to-run consistency. However, this comes with tradeoffs: without_skill was sometimes substantially faster and cheaper, and in the few evals with quality judging, without_skill was favored on accuracy/actionability criteria while with_skill was favored on completeness. Several basic assertions passed for both variants, indicating not all checks differentiate them, and quality-comparison data is sparse (4/11 evals) and only medium confidence, so conclusions about output quality specifically should be treated cautiously.
